name: Holded
tagline: Cloud ERP bundling invoicing, accounting, inventory, CRM, projects and payroll for small businesses, mostly in Spain.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: You can absolutely build an invoice generator and a transaction ledger in a day, and for a freelancer with ten invoices a month that might genuinely be enough. What you cannot build is the part people actually buy: legally compliant invoice series, Spanish tax model prefills, e-invoicing and anti-fraud certification regimes, bank feed connections, and an export your accountant will accept without sighing. The moment a tax authority or an external bookkeeper is downstream of your data, a hand-rolled SQLite app becomes a liability rather than a tool. Holded is also deliberately the union of six products, so a one-shot replacement means picking one of the six and quietly abandoning the rest. Build the invoicing slice if you want, but do not pretend it replaced the ERP.
coreLoopDIY: A local invoicing and expense ledger: clients, line-item invoices with sequential numbering, PDF export, expense entry, and a VAT summary per quarter.
requirements: a headless Chromium install for PDF rendering
your own tax rates and invoice numbering rules
an accountant who will accept a CSV
whatYouLose: Certified e-invoicing and anti-fraud compliance, which in Spain is not optional paperwork
Automatic bank feed imports and transaction reconciliation
Tax model prefills and the accountant-facing export formats
The other five modules: inventory, CRM, projects, HR, payroll
Audit trail, backups, and someone to blame when the numbers are wrong
moatNotes: Invoicing software in the EU is slowly becoming a regulated category. That is a moat you cannot code around in a weekend, only comply with.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the invoice is a legal document and the ledger is evidence. Small business owners pay Holded not for the UI but to outsource the question of whether their paperwork is acceptable to the tax office, and to hand their accountant something standard instead of a folder of CSVs. Add that it quietly replaces four or five separate subscriptions, and the per-month cost stops looking like software and starts looking like a very cheap junior bookkeeper.
notes: The invoice PDF is a weekend; the legal standing of that PDF is not. The moat is compliance certification plus the bank and accountant integrations that make your numbers someone else's problem.
prompt:
Build a local-first invoicing and expense ledger for a one-person business. No cloud, no accounts, no telemetry.

Stack, non-negotiable:
- Next.js 15 App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind. Single app, runs with `npm run dev` on localhost.
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, file at ./data/ledger.db, schema created on first boot with plain SQL migrations in /db.
- PDF generation with Puppeteer rendering a server-side HTML invoice template.
- Zod for all form validation. No ORM, no auth, no external APIs.

In scope:
- Clients: name, tax ID, address, email, default tax rate, notes. Full CRUD.
- Invoices: pick a client, add line items (description, quantity, unit price, tax rate per line), auto totals with per-rate tax breakdown, issue date, due date, status (draft, sent, paid).
- Invoice numbering: strictly sequential per calendar year, format INV-YYYY-0001, allocated only when an invoice leaves draft, never reused. Enforce this in SQL with a unique constraint.
- Immutability: once an invoice leaves draft it cannot be edited or deleted, only superseded by a credit note that references it.
- Expenses: date, vendor, category, net amount, tax amount, attached receipt file stored under ./data/receipts.
- Reports page: per-quarter summary of invoiced net, tax collected, expense net, tax paid, and net difference. Export as CSV.
- Company settings page: your own name, tax ID, address, logo upload, currency, default payment terms, invoice footer text.
- Seed script with 3 clients, 6 invoices across two quarters, and 10 expenses.

Out of scope, do not build: bank imports, OCR, multi-user, multi-currency conversion, inventory, CRM, payroll, email sending, recurring invoices, any e-invoicing or government filing format.

Put a banner in the settings page reading: "Not certified for e-invoicing. Check local rules before using these PDFs as legal invoices."

Any config goes in .env with a committed .env.example. Write a README with setup, the backup command (copy ./data), and an explicit list of what this does not do.
